fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of Progressive Muscle Relaxation, Deep Breathing, and Guided Imagery in Promoting Psychological and Physiological States of Relaxation Abstract Research suggests that multiple forms of relaxation training (e.g., progressive muscle relaxation, meditation, breathing exercises, visualization, and autogenics) can help individuals reduce stress, enhance relaxation states, and improve overall well-being. We examined three different, commonly used approaches to stress relaxation—progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, and guided imagery—and evaluated them in a head-to-head comparison against each other and a control condition. Sixty healthy undergraduate participants were randomized to one of the four conditions and completed 20 minutes of progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, or guided imagery training that was delivered by recorded audio instruction. Baseline and follow-up assessment of psychological relaxation states were completed. Physiological relaxation was also assessed continuously using measures of electrodermal activity and heart rate. Results showed that progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, and guided imagery all increased the state of relaxation for participants in those groups, compared to participants in the control group. In each case, the increase was statistically significant and although the groups did not differ on relaxation before training, all groups were significantly higher on relaxation after training, as compared to the control group. Progressive muscle relaxation and guided imagery showed an immediate linear trend toward physiological relaxation, compared to the control group, and the deep breathing group showed an immediate increase in physiological arousal followed quickly by a return to initial levels. Our results lend support to the body of research showing that stress relaxation training can be effective in improving relaxation states at both the psychological and physiological level. Future research could examine stress relaxation techniques in a similar manner using designs where multiple techniques can be compared in the same samples. 1. Introduction The present investigation seeks to better understand relaxation strategies by examining the efficacy of three different relaxation approaches in bringing about both psychological and physiological relaxation. Extant literature demonstrates the effectiveness of relaxation strategies, such as deep breathing, guided imagery, meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, and many other methods [1], but rarely are these strategies examined side-by-side in an experiment to evaluate relative effectiveness in promoting relaxation. It remains the case that we know only that many of these techniques are effective in promoting relaxation, not which techniques are most effective in bringing about relaxation. It is critically important that we better understand the most effective methods for increasing relaxation and the underlying self-regulation competencies because the relaxation response is directly and inversely related to chronic stress difficulties and poor mental and physical health [2–4]. The current study explores differences in the impact of progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing, and guided imagery, as compared to a control condition, on psychological and physiological relaxation states in an undergraduate student sample. We chose to examine deep breathing, guided imagery, and progressive muscle relaxation because these three methods can be easily taught and practiced using a standardized audio recording, they are known to be effective, and they can realize almost immediate benefits. While we expect that all three methods will elicit relaxation responses, differences among the techniques are less clear and will be carefully examined in this comparative effectiveness research. We begin with a brief review of these techniques and then summarize our present aims. 1.1. Progressive Muscle Relaxation Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) is an actively engaging relaxation technique developed by Edmund Jacobson in the 1920s [5]. PMR involves participants actively contracting muscles to create tension and progressively releasing this [6]. The routine is repeated until participants acquire complete relaxation. This technique utilizes the principles of neuronal “top-down” and “bottom-up” processing to achieve results [7]. In “top-down” processing, participants use areas higher in the nervous system like the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum to contract muscles and gradually release the tension. In “bottom-up” processing, the holding and releasing of bodily tension produce proprioceptive stimulation from peripheral muscles that ascends to the brain via the spinal cord and the brainstem. With both stimulatory passages activated, PMR provides participants with quick and immediate relief. The effects of this technique have been widely demonstrated in numerous studies. For instance, PMR can be useful in reducing stress. Pv and Lobo selected a simple random sample of 30 first-year nursing students, measured stress levels before and after PMR, and found a significant reduction in stress [8]. In another study with nursing students, PMR alleviated test anxiety [6], In this study, 49 students were randomized to a PMR treatment or control group, and both groups completed the Sarason Anxiety Questionnaire at baseline and completion of the experiment. The PMR treatment group received four 30-minute sessions of PMR. Although there was no significant difference before and after the experiment in the control group on test anxiety, a significant reduction in test anxiety was found in the treatment group. Not only does PMR demonstrate stress-alleviating effects, but also it exhibits a positive influence on depression and anxiety. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions Panic attacks and panic disorder Request an Appointment Print Overview A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear that triggers severe physical reactions when there is no real danger or apparent cause. Panic attacks can be very frightening. When panic attacks occur, you might think you're losing control, having a heart attack or even dying. Many people have just one or two panic attacks in their lifetimes, and the problem goes away, perhaps when a stressful situation ends. But if you've had recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and spent long periods in constant fear of another attack, you may have a condition called panic disorder. Although panic attacks themselves aren't life-threatening, they can be frightening and significantly affect your quality of life. But treatment can be very effective. Products & Services * A Book: Mayo Clinic Family Health Book * Newsletter: Mayo Clinic Health Letter — Digital Edition Show more products from Mayo Clinic Symptoms Panic attacks typically begin suddenly, without warning. They can strike at any time — when you're driving a car, at the mall, sound asleep or in the middle of a business meeting. You may have occasional panic attacks, or they may occur frequently. Panic attacks have many variations, but symptoms usually peak within minutes. You may feel fatigued and worn out after a panic attack subsides. Panic attacks typically include some of these signs or symptoms: * Sense of impending doom or danger. * Fear of loss of control or death. * Rapid, pounding heart rate. * Sweating. * Trembling or shaking. * Shortness of breath or tightness in your throat. * Chills. * Hot flashes. * Nausea. * Abdominal cramping. * Chest pain. * Headache. * Dizziness, lightheadedness or faintness. * Numbness or tingling sensation. * Feeling of unreality or detachment. One of the worst things about panic attacks is the intense fear that you'll have another one. You may fear having panic attacks so much that you avoid certain situations where they may occur. When to see a doctor If you have panic attack symptoms, seek medical help as soon as possible. Panic attacks, while intensely uncomfortable, are not dangerous. But panic attacks are hard to manage on your own, and they may get worse without treatment. Panic attack symptoms can also resemble symptoms of other serious health problems, such as a heart attack, so it's important to get evaluated by your primary care provider if you aren't sure what's causing your symptoms. fetched_contents.text: Ataques de pânico e síndrome do pânico - Distúrbios de saúde mental Um ataque de pânico é um período breve em que a pessoa sente angústia, ansiedade ou medo extremos, que têm início súbito e são acompanhados por sintomas físicos e/ou emocionais. A síndrome do pânico consiste em ataques de pânico recorrentes que causam uma preocupação excessiva com ataques futuros e/ou modificações de comportamento para evitar situações que poderiam desencadear um ataque. * Ataques de pânico podem causar sintomas como dor torácica, sensação de engasgo, tontura, náusea e falta de ar. * O diagnóstico baseia-se na descrição dos ataques feitos pela pessoa e no medo que manifestam de futuros ataques. * O tratamento pode incluir medicamentos antidepressivos, ansiolíticos, terapia de exposição e psicoterapia. Ataques de pânico são algo comum e ocorrem em pelo menos 11% dos adultos anualmente. A maioria das pessoas geralmente se recupera dos ataques de pânico sem tratamento, porém, algumas desenvolvem síndrome do pânico. Os ataques de pânico podem fazer parte de qualquer transtorno de ansiedade. Os ataques de pânico também podem ocorrer em pessoas com outros problemas de saúde mental (por exemplo, depressão). Alguns ataques de pânico ocorrem em resposta a uma situação específica. Por exemplo, uma pessoa com fobia de cobra pode entrar em pânico ao deparar-se com uma. Outros ataques ocorrem sem um fator desencadeador aparente. A síndrome do pânico está presente quando a pessoa se preocupa em ter outros ataques de pânico e/ou modifica seu comportamento para tentar evitar as crises. A síndrome do pânico ocorre em 2% a 3% da população anualmente. Mulheres têm duas vezes mais propensão de terem síndrome do pânico do que homens. A síndrome do pânico geralmente tem início no final da adolescência ou no início da idade adulta (ver Síndromes do pânico em crianças e adolescentes). Um ataque de pânico implica no surgimento súbito de medo ou desconforto intensos e, no mínimo, em quatro dos seguintes sintomas físicos e emocionais: * Dor ou desconforto no tórax * Uma sensação de engasgo * Vertigens, instabilidade postural ou desmaios * Medo de morrer * Medo de enlouquecer ou de perder o controle * Sensações de irrealidade, estranhamento ou distanciamento do meio em que vive * Agitação ou arrepios * Náuseas, dores gástricas ou diarreia * Sensação de dormência ou formigamento * Palpitações ou frequência cardíaca acelerada * Falta de ar ou sensação de asfixia * Sudorese * Tremores ou espasmos * Embora os ataques de pânico causem sintomas como falta de ar ou dor torácica, eles não são perigosos. Os sintomas de um ataque de pânico envolvem muitos tipos de sintomas físicos e as pessoas costumam pensar que têm algum problema de saúde grave afetando o coração, pulmões ou cérebro. Por exemplo, a dor no peito pode ocorrer durante um ataque de pânico e a pessoa pode ficar com medo de estar tendo um ataque cardíaco. Os sintomas graves ou persistentes devem ser avaliados por um médico. No entanto, é possível que uma pessoa consulte um médico ou vá ao pronto-socorro muitas vezes até que o diagnóstico correto de ataque de pânico seja feito. Embora os ataques de pânico causem incômodo, às vezes extremo, eles não são perigosos. Os sintomas geralmente atingem o pico em 10 minutos e desaparecem em alguns minutos, de modo que o médico talvez não consiga observá-los diretamente. Uma vez que o motivo dos ataques de pânico nem sempre é evidente, a pessoa que os apresenta geralmente prevê e se preocupa com a possibilidade de ter outro ataque – um quadro clínico denominado ansiedade antecipatória – e então tenta evitar as situações que ela associa à ocorrência de ataques de pânico anteriores. A frequência dos ataques pode variar muito. Algumas pessoas têm ataques semanais, ou até diários, que ocorrem durante meses, ao passo que outras têm vários ataques diários seguidos por semanas ou meses sem ataques. A síndrome do pânico costuma ser acompanhada por pelo menos mais um quadro clínico. Outros transtornos de ansiedade, transtorno depressivo maior, transtorno bipolar e transtorno por uso de álcool leve são os problemas de saúde mental concomitantes mais comuns. Os quadros clínicos concomitantes comuns incluem arritmia cardíaca, hipertireoidismo, asma e doença pulmonar obstrutiva crônica (DPOC). Diagnóstico de ataques de pânico e síndrome do pânico * Avaliação de um médico com base em critérios de diagnóstico psiquiátrico padrão Uma vez que doenças físicas graves frequentemente causam alguns dos mesmos sintomas físicos e emocionais observados em ataques de pânico, o médico primeiramente confirma que a pessoa não tem alguma doença física. O médico coleta informações sobre a experiência da pessoa com as crises e talvez faça exames para outros problemas. A síndrome do pânico é diagnosticada quando a pessoa apresenta ataques de pânico repetidos e inesperados combinados com, pelo menos, um dos fatores a seguir durante no mínimo um mês: * Preocupação persistente de que ela terá outros ataques de pânico ou preocupação com as consequências do ataque (por exemplo, de que ela perderá o controle ou irá enlouquecer) * Alterações no comportamento devido aos ataques de pânico (por exemplo, evitar situações que poderiam causar um ataque) Assim que o médico tiver confirmado que os sintomas da pessoa são causados por síndrome do pânico, ele tenta evitar fazer exames prolongados quando ataques de pânico ocorrem no futuro, a menos que os sintomas da pessoa ou os resultados de exame físico sugiram a existência um novo problema. Tratamento de ataques de pânico e síndrome do pânico * Antidepressivos e/ou medicamentos ansiolíticos * Psicoterapia, incluindo terapia de exposição, terapia cognitivo-comportamental e psicoterapia interpessoal Algumas pessoas se recuperam sem receber um tratamento formal, sobretudo se continuarem a confrontar as situações nas quais os ataques tenham ocorrido. Best non-pharmacologic relaxation strategies for panic attacks

The evidence points to several well-supported non-pharmacologic relaxation strategies, especially progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), deep breathing, and grounding/sensory-based methods. These approaches are especially useful during panic attacks because they target both psychological and physiological arousal, helping people interrupt the panic response and regain control [N1-F1][N1-R3].

### 1) Specific breathing techniques and how they work
Breathing exercises are among the most commonly recommended and accessible tools for panic attacks. The evidence base here is strongest for deep breathing and related relaxation breathing exercises. In the comparative review, deep breathing was found to increase psychological relaxation states compared to a control group, although it showed a more variable physiological response than PMR and guided imagery [N1-F1]. 

The practical logic is straightforward: during a panic attack, people often hyperventilate or become breathless, which can worsen anxiety and physical symptoms. Breathing exercises help restore normal breathing patterns, reduce hyperventilation, and promote a calming physiological state. They work by activating the parasympathetic nervous system through rhythmic, controlled breathing, which counteracts the fight-or-flight response [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The evidence also notes that breathing and relaxation exercises are recommended for stress, anxiety, and tension, with explicit guidance on how to do them [N1-R4].

### 2) Grounding exercises and sensory-based coping methods
The evidence set is thinner on grounding exercises, but the Brazilian source provides useful context: it describes practical steps for managing a panic attack, including “mudar de ambiente” (changing environment) and emphasizing that symptoms will pass [N4-R3]. While not a direct evidence source for grounding techniques, this fits the broader principle that sensory-based coping methods help anchor the person in the present moment and reduce the dominance of catastrophic thinking.

Grounding exercises such as the 5-4-3-2-1 technique, which engages the five senses, are a standard evidence-informed approach for acute anxiety and panic. The evidence here is not directly provided, but the broader relaxation literature supports sensory-based strategies as part of a comprehensive toolkit [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In a panic attack, grounding helps reduce the intensity of the emotional response by redirecting attention away from feared catastrophic outcomes and toward immediate sensory experiences [N4-R3].

### 3) Progressive muscle relaxation and body-scan approaches
Progressive muscle relaxation is the most clearly evidence-supported strategy in the provided materials. The review explicitly states that PMR increased psychological relaxation states and that it is an evidence-based technique involving tensing and relaxing different muscles around the body [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. It also explains the physiological mechanism: PMR uses both “top-down” and “bottom-up” processing, where tension and release produce proprioceptive stimulation that ascends through the spinal cord and brainstem, helping participants achieve quick and immediate relief [N1-F1].

Body-scan approaches are closely related to PMR but are often used as a mindfulness-based body awareness practice rather than a muscle-tensing sequence. While the provided evidence does not explicitly name body-scan, it does support the general idea of using body awareness to interrupt panic and promote relaxation. The evidence base here is stronger for PMR than for body-scan specifically, so it should be framed as a closely related but slightly different approach [N1-R2][N1-F1].

### Practical takeaway
For a patient seeking non-pharmacologic strategies, the strongest recommendations are:
- **Deep breathing** as a fast-acting way to regulate breathing and calm physiological arousal [N1-F1][N1-R4]
- **Progressive muscle relaxation** as a structured, evidence-based technique for reducing tension and promoting relaxation [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]
- **Sensory-based grounding** as a practical way to stay present during an attack [N4-R3]

The evidence suggests that these methods work best when practiced regularly and used during the early stages of an attack rather than waiting for symptoms to escalate. They are also best combined with education about panic attack biology and cognitive restructuring, as the provided Brazilian context emphasizes the need to avoid avoidance and recognize that symptoms are temporary [N4-F3].

When to seek professional help and safety guidance

The evidence here is divided into two parts: the immediate emergency/red-flag signs and the broader guidance on when to consult a doctor versus self-manage. The Brazilian/Portuguese source is especially important for practical context, while the general panic attack sources provide the medical criteria [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### 1) Red flags indicating a need for immediate medical care
The strongest red flags are symptoms that suggest a serious physical problem rather than a panic attack alone. The Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or lose consciousness, you should seek emergency medical care [N3-F2]. It also emphasizes that panic attacks can resemble symptoms of a heart attack, so it is important to get evaluated by a primary care provider if symptoms are unclear [N3-F2]. The NHS source lists similar physical symptoms of panic attacks, including chest pain, sweating, nausea, shortness of breath, trembling, hot flushes, and dizziness, and notes that panic attacks are not dangerous but should be managed promptly [N3-R2].

The Brazilian source adds practical red flags: it says that people may go to the emergency room multiple times before the correct diagnosis is made, and that symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting should prompt medical help [N4-F3]. It also notes that people may fear having a heart attack or dying during an attack, which can increase distress and reinforce avoidance behavior [N4-F3].

### 2) When to consult a doctor versus self-manage
The evidence supports a staged approach. If symptoms are new, severe, or unclear, or if they significantly interfere with daily life, a doctor should be consulted. The Mayo Clinic source says to seek medical help as soon as possible if you have panic attack symptoms, because panic attacks are not dangerous but can be difficult to manage without treatment [N3-F2]. The NHS source similarly advises seeking help early if symptoms are persistent or worrying [N3-R2].

For self-management, the evidence suggests that acute panic attack strategies such as breathing, grounding, and PMR are appropriate during an attack [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The Brazilian source also supports practical self-help measures, including changing environment and reassuring oneself that symptoms will pass [N4-R3]. However, the evidence does not support relying on self-management alone if symptoms are recurrent, frequent, or interfere with functioning. In that case, professional help is indicated [N4-F3].

### 3) Practical steps to reduce panic attack frequency and severity
The evidence-based practical steps include:
- **Early intervention**: Use breathing or grounding techniques as soon as an attack begins [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R3]
- **Avoidance of catastrophic thinking**: The Brazilian source notes that people often fear losing control or dying, which can worsen panic [N4-F3]
- **Education and reassurance**: The sources repeatedly stress that panic attacks are not dangerous and will pass, which is important for reducing fear and avoidance [N3-F2][N4-F3]
- **Behavioral modification**: The Brazilian source emphasizes that some people recover without treatment if they confront situations where attacks have occurred, while others may need professional help [N4-F3]
- **Medical evaluation**: The Mayo Clinic source says to consult a provider if symptoms are unclear or persistent [N3-F2]

### Bottom line
If the patient experiences chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or repeated, severe attacks that interfere with life, immediate medical evaluation is strongly indicated [N3-F2][N4-F3]. For less severe or episodic attacks, self-management with breathing, grounding, and PMR is appropriate, but the evidence supports seeking professional help if symptoms persist, worsen, or are confusing [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-F2]. The practical guidance also emphasizes that panic attacks are often not dangerous, but they can be distressing and difficult to manage without support [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Pharmacologic vs non-pharmacologic boundaries and realistic expectations

The evidence suggests a clear distinction between non-receita (non-prescription) remedies and pharmacologic options, while also emphasizing that panic attack management should be personalized. The OTC/supplement evidence is broader but less definitive than the relaxation and safety evidence, whereas the medical sources make clear that panic attacks are not inherently life-threatening but can be distressing and may require treatment [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-F2][N4-F3].

### 1) What is realistic to expect from non-receita remedies
The available evidence indicates that non-receita remedies can help in the short term but are not a substitute for professional care. For example, the OTC/natural remedies source lists magnesium, kava kava, and chamomile as natural remedies with promising research on stress and anxiety [N2-R1]. Another source states that melatonin and magnesium may help in the short term, but they are not a cure and may carry risks [N2-R3]. The Brazilian source also mentions non-prescription remedies for anxiety, including chás de passiflora, valeriana, and camomila, but emphasizes that they should be used with professional guidance [N5-R2].

So, the realistic expectations are:
- Some OTC/supplements may reduce anxiety or improve sleep temporarily [N2-R1][N2-R3]
- They are not proven to be universally effective for panic attacks, and evidence is mixed or limited [N2-R1][N2-R5]
- They can be part of a self-management toolkit, but they should not delay or replace medical evaluation [N2-R3][N3-F2]

### 2) Where pharmacologic options fit and why they are not the same as OTC remedies
The evidence shows that pharmacologic options are more targeted and generally more effective for recurrent or severe panic attacks. The Brazilian source notes that treatment may include antidepressants, anxiolytics, exposure therapy, and psychotherapy [N4-F3]. The MSD source also says that the majority of people recover without treatment, but some develop panic disorder, which may need medical treatment [N4-F3].

Pharmacologic options are not the same as OTC remedies because:
- They are usually prescription medications, such as benzodiazepines, antidepressants, or other anxiolytics, rather than simple over-the-counter products [N4-F3][N4-R2]
- They are intended for more persistent or severe symptoms, whereas OTC remedies are intended for mild or situational support [N2-R3][N2-R5]
- They are part of a structured treatment plan that may include psychotherapy and behavioral interventions [N4-F3]

### 3) How panic attack management should be personalized
The evidence supports a personalized approach. The Brazilian source notes that treatment may vary depending on whether symptoms are episodic or recurrent, and that some people recover without treatment while others need formal intervention [N4-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly emphasizes that treatment can be very effective and that symptoms can resemble other serious conditions, so evaluation by a provider is important [N3-F2]. The relaxation evidence also supports individualized practice: the comparative study found that PMR, deep breathing, and guided imagery all increased relaxation, but the evidence base was not enough to establish a single “best” technique for everyone [N1-F1].

In practical terms, personalization means:
- Choosing relaxation techniques that fit the person’s lifestyle and preferences [N1-F1][N1-R2]
- Using OTC/supplements cautiously and under guidance, especially if symptoms are recurrent or severe [N2-R1][N2-R3]
- Seeking medical help when symptoms are persistent, frequent, or interfere with daily life [N3-F2][N4-F3]

### Bottom line
Non-receita remedies can offer short-term support for mild anxiety or panic symptoms, but they are not a substitute for professional care [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Pharmacologic options are more appropriate for recurrent or severe panic attacks and are part of a broader treatment plan that may include psychotherapy and behavioral strategies [N4-F3]. The best management approach is personalized: some people may do well with self-management and OTC support, while others need medical evaluation and treatment [N3-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1].

OTC options and supplements that may help with panic attack symptoms

The evidence base for OTC options and supplements is broader than it is definitive, but it does identify several commonly used products with some supporting evidence or common use. The strongest evidence points to magnesium and melatonin as short-term sleep/anxiety aids, while valeriana, passiflora, and chamomila are mentioned as natural options in Brazilian sources [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N5-R2]. The evidence also cautions that these products may carry risks and should not be relied on as a substitute for medical evaluation [N2-R3][N3-F2].

### 1) Which OTC products have the strongest evidence or common use
The most consistently mentioned OTC/supplement options are:

- **Magnesium**: The strongest evidence-supported option in the provided materials. It is described as helping manage anxiety and insomnia by regulating serotonin and improving brain function, and as a short-term aid for anxiety symptoms [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It is also listed as one of the top OTC supplements with potential anxiolytic benefits [N2-R5].
- **Melatonin**: This is commonly used for sleep and is mentioned as an over-the-counter sleep aid that may help in the short term, though it is not a cure and may carry risks [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Valeriana, passiflora, and camomila**: These are natural remedies often recommended in Brazilian sources for anxiety and panic-related symptoms [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- **Kava kava and chamomile**: These are highlighted as natural remedies with promising research on stress and anxiety [N2-R1].

### 2) Possible benefits and limitations of each option
- **Magnesium**
  - **Benefits**: May help manage anxiety and insomnia, and is commonly used as a short-term aid [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]
  - **Limitations**: Evidence is not strong enough to prove consistent or universal effectiveness, and it can interact with certain medications or cause side effects such as diarrhea [N2-R3]
- **Melatonin**
  - **Benefits**: May help with sleep, which can reduce anxiety and panic symptoms [N2-R3][N2-R4]
  - **Limitations**: Not a cure, and sleep aids may not address the root cause of panic attacks; also, excessive use can cause drowsiness, grogginess, or dependence [N2-R3][N2-R4]
- **Valeriana, passiflora, and camomila**
  - **Benefits**: Commonly used for mild anxiety and are often preferred by people who want non-receita options [N5-R2][N5-R4]
  - **Limitations**: Evidence for panic-specific effectiveness is limited, and they may cause drowsiness or interact with other medications [N2-R1][N5-R4]
- **Kava kava and chamomile**
  - **Benefits**: Promising research on stress and anxiety [N2-R1]
  - **Limitations**: Kava kava has safety concerns and may not be suitable for long-term use; chamomile is generally safer but still not a proven cure [N2-R1][N5-R4]

### 3) Warnings about safety and interactions
The evidence repeatedly warns that these products are not a substitute for medical care. The OTC sleep aid source states that short-term use may help, but the products are not a cure and may carry risks [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The Brazilian sources caution that natural remedies should be used with professional guidance, and that some products may have interactions or safety concerns [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Important safety considerations include:
- **Interactions with medications**: Magnesium, valeriana, and other supplements may interact with antidepressants, blood pressure medications, or sedatives [N2-R3][N5-R4]
- **Side effects**: Drowsiness, grogginess, gastrointestinal upset, and in some cases, more serious effects [N2-R3][N5-R4]
- **Quality and dosage**: Natural products may vary widely in potency and purity, so it is important to use them cautiously and under guidance [N2-R1][N5-R4]
- **Not a substitute for evaluation**: If symptoms are recurrent, severe, or unclear, medical evaluation is still needed [N2-R3][N3-F2]

### Bottom line
For OTC/supplement options, magnesium appears to have the strongest evidence and common use for mild anxiety and sleep support, while valeriana, passiflora, camomila, kava kava, and chamomile are more commonly used but with less consistent evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. The safest approach is to use these products cautiously, understand their limitations, and consult a healthcare provider before relying on them long-term [N2-R3][N3-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## 1) Best relaxation strategies to use during a panic attack

The strongest evidence supports several non-pharmacologic relaxation strategies. These are especially useful during a panic attack because they help interrupt the panic response and bring the body back to a calmer state [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R2].

### A) Breathing exercises
Breathing is one of the most immediate and practical tools. The evidence shows that deep breathing increases psychological relaxation states and is recommended for stress, anxiety, and tension [N1-F1][N1-R4]. During a panic attack, people often hyperventilate, which can worsen symptoms, so breathing exercises help restore normal breathing and reduce physiological arousal [N1-R4].

**How it works:**  
You breathe slowly and deliberately, usually through the nose and out through the mouth, to activate the parasympathetic nervous system and counteract the fight-or-flight response [N1-R2][N1-R4].

### B) Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR)
PMR is the most clearly evidence-supported strategy in the provided materials. It involves tensing and relaxing different muscle groups, and the review found that it increased psychological relaxation states compared to a control group [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1].

**How it works:**  
PMR uses both “top-down” and “bottom-up” processing. Tensing muscles creates tension, and releasing them produces proprioceptive stimulation that helps calm the nervous system [N1-F1]. It is especially useful for reducing tension and promoting relaxation during an attack.

### C) Grounding exercises and sensory-based coping
The evidence is a bit thinner on grounding exercises, but the Brazilian source provides useful practical context: it says people may “mudar de ambiente” (change environment) and reassure themselves that symptoms will pass [N4-R3]. This fits the broader principle that grounding helps anchor the person in the present moment and reduces catastrophic thinking.

Grounding exercises such as the 5-4-3-2-1 technique are standard evidence-informed methods for acute anxiety and panic. While not directly proven in the provided materials, the relaxation literature supports these as part of a comprehensive toolkit [N1-R2][N1-R4].

### Practical takeaway for panic attacks
During a panic attack, the best sequence is usually:
1. **Breathe deeply** to calm breathing and reduce hyperventilation [N1-F1][N1-R4]
2. **Use PMR** if the person can do it quickly [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]
3. **Use grounding** to stay present and reduce fear [N4-R3]

These strategies work best when practiced regularly and used early in an attack, not waited for until symptoms are severe.

## 2) Non-receita remedies and supplements that may help with panic attack symptoms

The evidence suggests that OTC/supplement options can be part of a self-management toolkit, but they are not a substitute for medical evaluation [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F2].

### A) Which OTC products have the strongest evidence or common use?
The most consistently mentioned options are:

- **Magnesium**: Evidence suggests it may help manage anxiety and insomnia by regulating serotonin and brain function, and it is listed as one of the top OTC supplements with potential anxiolytic benefits [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].
- **Melatonin**: It is commonly used as an over-the-counter sleep aid and may help in the short term, although it is not a cure and may carry risks [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Valeriana, passiflora, and camomila**: These are natural remedies often recommended in Brazilian sources for anxiety and panic-related symptoms [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- **Kava kava and chamomile**: These are mentioned as natural remedies with promising research on stress and anxiety [N2-R1].

### B) Benefits and limitations of each option
- **Magnesium**: May help anxiety and insomnia, but evidence is not strong enough to prove consistent or universal effectiveness; may cause side effects or interact with medications [N2-R2][N2-R3][N5-R4].
- **Melatonin**: May help sleep, which can reduce anxiety, but it is not a cure and may cause drowsiness, grogginess, or dependence [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Valeriana, passiflora, and camomila**: Commonly used for mild anxiety but with limited panic-specific evidence; may cause drowsiness or interact with medications [N5-R2][N5-R4].
- **Kava kava and chamomile**: Promising for stress and anxiety, but kava kava has safety concerns and may not be suitable for long-term use [N2-R1][N5-R4].

### C) Warnings about safety and interactions
The evidence repeatedly warns that these products should not be relied on as a substitute for medical care. OTC sleep aids are not a cure and may carry risks [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Brazilian sources also caution that natural remedies should be used with professional guidance, especially because they may interact with other medications or have safety concerns [N5-R2][N5-R4].

Important safety points:
- **Interactions with medications**: Magnesium, valeriana, and other supplements may interact with antidepressants, blood pressure medications, or sedatives [N2-R3][N5-R4]
- **Side effects**: Drowsiness, grogginess, gastrointestinal upset, and in some cases, more serious effects [N2-R3][N5-R4]
- **Quality and dosage**: Natural products can vary widely in potency and purity [N2-R1][N5-R4]
- **Not a substitute for evaluation**: If symptoms are recurrent, severe, or unclear, medical evaluation is still needed [N2-R3][N3-F2]

### Bottom line on OTC remedies
Magnesium appears to have the strongest evidence and common use for mild anxiety and sleep support, while valeriana, passiflora, camomila, kava kava, and chamomile are more commonly used but with less consistent evidence [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. The safest approach is to use these products cautiously, understand their limitations, and consult a healthcare provider before relying on them long-term [N2-R3][N3-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## 3) When to seek professional help and safety guidance

The evidence clearly separates red flags from routine self-management. Panic attacks are not life-threatening, but they can be very distressing and may require medical help if they recur, worsen, or are confusing [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### A) Red flags indicating immediate medical care
The strongest red flags are symptoms that suggest a serious physical problem rather than a panic attack alone:
- chest pain
- trouble breathing
- fainting
- severe, prolonged symptoms that do not clearly match a panic attack pattern [N3-F2][N4-F3]

The Mayo Clinic source says to seek emergency medical care if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or lose consciousness [N3-F2]. It also notes that panic attacks can resemble heart attack symptoms, so it is important to get evaluated by a primary care provider if symptoms are unclear [N3-F2].

The Brazilian source adds that people may go to the emergency room multiple times before the correct diagnosis is made, which is an important practical reminder [N4-F3].

### B) When to consult a doctor versus self-manage
If symptoms are new, severe, or unclear, or if they significantly interfere with daily life, a doctor should be consulted [N3-F2]. The evidence supports early medical help because panic attacks are not dangerous but can be difficult to manage without treatment [N3-F2].

For self-management, the evidence supports using breathing, grounding, and PMR during an attack [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The Brazilian source also supports practical self-help measures, including changing environment and reassuring oneself that symptoms will pass [N4-R3].

### C) Practical steps to reduce panic attack frequency and severity
The evidence-based practical steps include:
- **Early intervention**: Use breathing or grounding techniques as soon as an attack begins [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R3]
- **Avoid catastrophic thinking**: The Brazilian source notes that people often fear losing control or dying, which can worsen panic [N4-F3]
- **Education and reassurance**: The sources repeatedly stress that panic attacks are not dangerous and will pass, which is important for reducing fear and avoidance [N3-F2][N4-F3]

### Bottom line on when to seek help
If the patient experiences chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or repeated, severe attacks that interfere with daily life, immediate medical evaluation is strongly indicated [N3-F2][N4-F3]. For less severe or episodic attacks, self-management with breathing, grounding, and PMR is appropriate, but the evidence supports seeking professional help if symptoms persist, worsen, or are confusing [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-F2]. The practical guidance also emphasizes that panic attacks are often not dangerous, but they can be distressing and difficult to manage without support [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 4) Pharmacologic vs non-pharmacologic boundaries and realistic expectations

The evidence suggests a clear distinction between non-receita remedies and pharmacologic options, while also emphasizing that panic attack management should be personalized [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

### A) What is realistic to expect from non-receita remedies
The available evidence indicates that non-receita remedies can help in the short term, but they are not a substitute for professional care [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F2]. They may reduce mild anxiety or improve sleep temporarily, but they are not proven to be universally effective for panic attacks [N2-R1][N2-R5].

### B) Where pharmacologic options fit and why they are not the same as OTC remedies
Pharmacologic options are more targeted and generally more effective for recurrent or severe panic attacks. The Brazilian source notes that treatment may include antidepressants, anxiolytics, exposure therapy, and psychotherapy [N4-F3]. The MSD source also says that the majority of people recover without treatment, but some develop panic disorder, which may need medical treatment [N4-F3].

Pharmacologic options are not the same as OTC remedies because:
- They are usually prescription medications, such as benzodiazepines, antidepressants, or other anxiolytics, rather than simple over-the-counter products [N4-F3][N4-R2]
- They are intended for more persistent or severe symptoms, whereas OTC remedies are intended for mild or situational support [N2-R3][N2-R5]
- They are part of a structured treatment plan that may include psychotherapy and behavioral interventions [N4-F3]

### C) How panic attack management should be personalized
The evidence supports a personalized approach. The Brazilian source notes that treatment may vary depending on whether symptoms are episodic or recurrent, and that some people recover without treatment while others need formal intervention [N4-F3]. The Mayo Clinic source similarly emphasizes that treatment can be very effective and that symptoms can resemble other serious conditions, so evaluation by a provider is important [N3-F2]. In practical terms, personalization means:
- Choosing relaxation techniques that fit the person’s lifestyle and preferences [N1-F1][N1-R2]

- Seeking medical help when symptoms are persistent, frequent, or interfere with daily life [N3-F2][N4-F3]

### Bottom line on pharmacologic vs non-pharmacologic
Non-receita remedies can offer short-term support for mild anxiety or panic symptoms, but they are not a substitute for professional care [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Pharmacologic options are more appropriate for recurrent or severe panic attacks and are part of a broader treatment plan that may include psychotherapy and behavioral strategies [N4-F3].
